headline: Can studying after a test improve the score you already got?
title: Feeling the Future: Experimental Evidence for Anomalous Retroactive Influences on Cognition and Affect
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants took a word-recall test. Only afterward did the computer randomly select words for them to practice. The author reported that participants had recalled more of the words they would later practice.

headline: Does holding hot coffee make a stranger seem warmer?
title: Experiencing Physical Warmth Promotes Interpersonal Warmth
note: On the way to the lab, participants briefly held someone else's hot or iced coffee. Those who held the hot cup later rated a person described in writing as having a warmer personality.

headline: Can striking a power pose raise your testosterone?
title: Power Posing: Brief Nonverbal Displays Affect Neuroendocrine Levels and Risk Tolerance
note: Participants held expansive or contracted poses, gave saliva samples and decided whether to gamble. The authors linked expansive poses to higher testosterone, lower cortisol and a greater willingness to take risks.

headline: Does a guilty conscience make a wet wipe more appealing?
title: Washing Away Your Sins: Threatened Morality and Physical Cleansing
note: The authors asked people to recall an unethical act and examined their interest in cleaning products. In another experiment, they compared how often people volunteered to help after either wiping their hands or leaving them alone.

headline: After a disgusting film clip, does washing your hands make you judge others less harshly?
title: With a Clean Conscience: Cleanliness Reduces the Severity of Moral Judgments
note: After watching a clip meant to provoke disgust, some participants washed their hands. The authors reported that those who washed up gave more lenient judgments when presented with a series of moral dilemmas.

headline: Is the cartoon funnier if you hold a pen between your teeth?
title: Inhibiting and Facilitating Conditions of the Human Smile: A Nonobtrusive Test of the Facial Feedback Hypothesis
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants rated cartoons while holding a pen with their teeth or their lips, putting their facial muscles in different positions. The original study reported that the teeth group found the cartoons funnier.

headline: Can the word “Florida” slow your walk down the hall?
title: Automaticity of Social Behavior: Direct Effects of Trait Construct and Stereotype Activation on Action
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants unscrambled sentences containing words associated with American stereotypes of older people, including “Florida.” The authors reported that people exposed to those words walked more slowly as they left the lab.

headline: Before trivia night, should you spend a few minutes thinking about a professor?
title: The Relation Between Perception and Behavior, or How to Win a Game of Trivial Pursuit
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: People thought about either professors or soccer hooligans and then answered general-knowledge questions. The authors reported that the professor group got more answers right.

headline: If you resist the cookies and eat radishes, will you give up sooner on a puzzle?
title: Ego Depletion: Is the Active Self a Limited Resource?
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants faced radishes and tempting treats. The authors reported that people allowed to eat only radishes gave up sooner on a subsequent unsolvable puzzle, and argued that exercising self-control had depleted a limited resource.

headline: Same photo, red background. More attractive?
title: Romantic Red: Red Enhances Men's Attraction to Women
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Researchers changed the colors surrounding photos or the colors of women's clothing and asked men to rate attractiveness. The authors reported higher ratings in several of the red conditions.

headline: Same golf ball. Call it lucky and more putts go in?
title: Keep Your Fingers Crossed!: How Superstition Improves Performance
note: Researchers told some participants that the golf ball they were about to use was lucky. The original paper reported that these participants sank more putts.

headline: Spatial reasoning test coming up? Cue Mozart.
title: Music and Spatial Task Performance
note: College students took spatial reasoning tests after listening to a Mozart sonata for two pianos, hearing relaxation instructions or sitting in silence. The paper reported a short-lived advantage after Mozart.

headline: Can reading a few pages of literary fiction help you read someone's eyes?
title: Reading Literary Fiction Improves Theory of Mind
note: After reading short texts, participants took social cognition tests. One showed only a person's eyes and asked which word best described their mental state. The authors interpreted the literary fiction group's performance as an improvement in theory of mind.

headline: Can a glimpse of Rodin's Thinker shake your faith?
title: Analytic Thinking Promotes Religious Disbelief
note: In one experiment, participants saw photographs of The Thinker or a discus thrower before rating their religious beliefs. The authors interpreted a difference in ratings as evidence that prompting analytical thinking weakens belief.

headline: Are hurricanes deadlier when they have women's names?
title: Female Hurricanes Are Deadlier Than Male Hurricanes
note: The authors analyzed historical US hurricane records and asked participants to judge hypothetical storms with different names. They argued that more feminine names make people underestimate danger and take fewer precautions.

headline: Can a red or pink shirt give away where you are in your cycle?
title: Women Are More Likely to Wear Red or Pink at Peak Fertility
note: Researchers estimated the likelihood of conception from menstrual cycle dates and compared it with the shirt color participants reported wearing. The paper reported more red or pink shirts in the higher-fertility group.

headline: Did support for Obama depend on the time of the month?
title: The Fluctuating Female Vote: Politics, Religion, and the Ovulatory Cycle
note: During the 2012 US presidential election, researchers compared women's political preferences with their reported menstrual cycles and relationship status. They reported that single women were more likely to support Barack Obama when estimated fertility was higher.

headline: So hungry you could use a few more binder clips?
title: Hunger Promotes Acquisition of Nonfood Objects
note: Researchers used office binder clips to test whether hunger changes how people acquire things they cannot eat. They reported that hungrier participants took more clips without saying they liked them any better.

headline: Does a heavier clipboard make a job applicant seem more important?
title: Incidental Haptic Sensations Influence Social Judgments and Decisions
note: Participants evaluated job applicants while holding lighter or heavier clipboards. The authors reported that the weight influenced the evaluations. Other experiments used rough puzzles and hard or soft chairs to test social judgments and bargaining decisions.

headline: Does a reminder of money make you less helpful?
title: The psychological consequences of money
note: Across nine experiments, the authors reported that cues associated with money reduced help-seeking and helping, and increased preferences for solitary activities.

headline: Does dimming the lights make people cheat?
title: Good lamps are the best police: darkness increases dishonesty and self-interested behavior
note: Participants completing a task under dim lighting reportedly claimed more unearned money than those in brighter surroundings.

headline: Can thinking about time instead of money make you more honest?
title: Time, money, and morality
note: The authors reported that reminders of money increased cheating, whereas reminders of time reduced it in experimental tasks.

headline: Can you wash away your buyer's remorse?
title: Washing away postdecisional dissonance
note: Handwashing after choosing between alternatives was reported to reduce the tendency to subsequently justify one's choice.

headline: Can a glimpse of red hurt your test score?
title: Color and psychological functioning: the effect of red on performance attainment
note: The authors reported poorer achievement-task performance following brief exposure to red compared with control colors.

headline: Can just reading the word RED make you worse at reasoning?
title: The semantic red effect: Processing the word red undermines intellectual performance
note: Four experiments reportedly found poorer intellectual task performance after processing the word red.

headline: Can the smell of cleaner make you clean up your crumbs?
title: Smells like clean spirit. Nonconscious effects of scent on cognition and behavior
note: Participants exposed to a cleaning-product scent reportedly removed more crumbs while eating than those without the scent.

headline: Does typing your notes make you learn less?
title: The pen is mightier than the keyboard: advantages of longhand over laptop note taking
note: The authors reported that laptop note takers performed worse on conceptual questions than longhand note takers in their lecture experiments.

headline: Does a heavier clipboard make fairness more important?
title: Weight as an Embodiment of Importance
note: The authors reported that clipboard weight changed ratings of monetary value and the importance of fair procedures.

headline: Does being left out make the room feel colder?
title: Cold and Lonely: Does Social Exclusion Literally Feel Cold?
note: Participants recalled social exclusion or inclusion. The authors reported lower estimated room temperatures after exclusion and greater preference for warm food and drinks in a separate experiment.

headline: Can a fishy smell make you distrust a stranger?
title: Bidirectionality, mediation, and moderation of metaphorical effects: the embodiment of social suspicion and fishy smells
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors linked incidental fish odors with reduced cooperation in economic games, interpreting the result through the metaphor of suspicion.

headline: Can a reminder of God make you give away more money?
title: God is watching you: priming God concepts increases prosocial behavior in an anonymous economic game
note: Participants completed a word task and then allocated money in an anonymous game. The authors reported more generous allocations after religious cues.

headline: Does cleaning your hands make you MORE judgmental?
title: A clean self can render harsh moral judgment
note: The authors reported harsher moral evaluations after participants cleaned their hands or imagined themselves clean.

headline: Can your bathing habits reveal loneliness?
title: The Substitutability of Physical and Social Warmth in Daily Life
note: The researchers linked self-reported loneliness to more frequent, longer and warmer baths or showers in one student sample.

headline: Does the smell of fish protect your memory from misinformation?
title: Resisting misinformation via discrepancy detection: effects of an unaware suspicion cue
note: The authors used fishy or neutral room odors during exposure to misleading information to investigate whether suspicion cues affect memory errors.

headline: Does liking sweets make you a sweeter person?
title: Sweet taste preferences and experiences predict prosocial inferences, personalities, and behaviors
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors related a preference for sweet foods to prosocial personality measures, intentions and behaviors.

headline: Can counting money make physical pain hurt less?
title: The symbolic power of money: reminders of money alter social distress and physical pain
note: The authors reported that reminders of money reduced distress from social exclusion and ratings of physical pain.

headline: Do lap dancers earn more tips near ovulation?
title: Ovulatory cycle effects on tip earnings by lap dancers: economic evidence for human estrus?
note: The authors compared self-reported tips and menstrual cycle timing among 18 dancers.

headline: Can men smell when ovulation is approaching?
title: Body odor attractiveness as a cue of impending ovulation in women: evidence from a study using hormone-confirmed ovulation
note: Men rated scent samples collected at different points in women's cycles.

headline: Do women dress more attractively near ovulation?
title: Ovulatory shifts in human female ornamentation: near ovulation, women dress to impress
note: The study compared photographs of women taken during different cycle phases.

headline: Can men spot fertility from the way women dance or walk?
title: Women’s body movements are a potential cue to ovulation
note: Men rated movement silhouettes from recordings at two cycle phases.

headline: Does a woman's face look better during her fertile phase?
title: Female facial attractiveness increases during the fertile phase of the menstrual cycle
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
note: The authors compared ratings of facial attractiveness at different cycle phases.

headline: Can a bad smell make you more morally judgmental?
title: Disgust as embodied moral judgment
note: The experiments exposed people to incidental disgust and recorded moral ratings.

headline: Can guilt make your body feel heavier?
title: The Weight of a Guilty Conscience: Subjective Body Weight as an Embodiment of Guilt
note: Participants' reported sense of body weight was compared after recalling different actions.
